491.title: With great joy (Luke 24:50–53)
491.hook: he blesses them as he's carried up, and they return with great joy
491.tomorrow: In the beginning was the Word
491.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension of the Lord forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many dioceses), and the Mass ends each time with the priest blessing the people before they are sent out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last evening in that room: he opened their understanding. Your line was opened. What did you reread and see differently? Day four hundred ninety-one, and the last page of Luke.

How do you say goodbye to someone you will not see again in this life? Most of us have stood at that edge: an airport curb, a hospital bed, a last visit with a grandparent. The goodbye usually leaves you emptied out. You drive home quiet. You sit in the car before you go inside. Luke's Gospel ends with a goodbye too. But the people in it don't go home quiet. They go home, of all things, happy. Today we read the last four verses of Luke, and the strange joy at the end of them.
screen: `THE LAST GOODBYE.` → `MOST OF US GO HOME QUIET.` → `THESE GO HOME HAPPY.`

segments.voice: Here's the ending, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he led them out as far as Bethania: and lifting up his hands, he blessed them." Then, while he is blessing them, he is parted from them and carried up to heaven. His last gesture in this Gospel is a blessing. Hands lifted, the way a priest blesses, and he is still doing it as he goes. And then: "And they adoring went back into Jerusalem with great joy." They had every reason for grief. Instead, joy. Why? Luke has told us. He gave them understanding. He promised power from on high. And he left blessing them, which means the last thing they saw was not his absence but his care. Now look at where Luke ends. In the temple. They were always in the temple, praising and blessing God. Do you remember where this Gospel began, about fifty days ago on this path? In the temple, with an old priest named Zachary, struck silent at the altar, unable to give the blessing. Luke opens with a blessing that couldn't be spoken, and closes with a blessing given and people blessing God in return. And between them, the whole Gospel: the angel and Mary, the manger, the boy in the temple, the sermon at Nazareth, the lost and found, the cross, the road to Emmaus. Joy runs through it, from the angel's good tidings of great joy at Bethlehem to this last line. Luke isn't finished, though. He wrote a second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, and it opens by telling the ascension again, more fully, with forty days and a cloud. Catholics celebrate that day as the Ascension of the Lord.
screen: `HE LIFTS HIS HANDS AND BLESSES.` · `THEY RETURN WITH GREAT JOY.` · `IT ENDS WHERE IT BEGAN, THE TEMPLE.` · `LUKE GOES ON IN ACTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end the day blessing someone. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone you said goodbye to today, even an ordinary goodbye: a kid at school drop-off, a coworker leaving, a parent on the phone. Picture them going on with their evening. Now wish them good, on purpose. Their sleep, their worries, their tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask God to bless them by name. If you don't, just send them the wish. Let the last thing you hold tonight be care, not absence. The bell holds the time.
With great joy. How the disciples went back to Jerusalem after Jesus blessed them and was carried up: the last line of Luke's story. Today's word.

Your line: great joy. Tonight, make your last word to someone a blessing. And that's the Gospel of Luke, fifty days, from Zachary in the temple to great joy in the temple. Tomorrow, John begins. Day four hundred ninety-one.
screen: `LUKE: FROM THE TEMPLE TO THE TEMPLE.`
`DAY 491 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.`

492.title: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1–5)
492.hook: the light shines in darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it
492.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's prologue at the Mass of Christmas Day, and again on the Second Sunday after Christmas where that Sunday is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page of Luke: a blessing on a hill, and disciples going home with great joy. Who got your blessing last night? Day four hundred ninety-two, and a new Gospel.

Matthew starts with a family tree. Mark starts with a man shouting in the desert. Luke starts with an old priest in the temple. John starts before anything started. No Bethlehem, no shepherds, no Jordan River. Just: in the beginning. If those words sound familiar, they should. They are the first words of the whole Bible, the opening of Genesis, before light, before land, before anyone. John borrows them on purpose. For the next six weeks we read the fourth Gospel in order, and on day one it reaches back past the first day of creation.
screen: `MATTHEW: A FAMILY TREE.` → `MARK: A VOICE IN THE DESERT.` → `JOHN: BEFORE ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Today's word is the one John uses, logos. In Greek it means a word, but also reason, an account, the meaning behind things. Greek philosophers had used logos for the order running through the universe. Jewish readers knew of God's word that creates, and of Wisdom, who was with God at the making of the world. John takes all of that and says something none of them said: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Then: "All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing that was made." Not a thing in your kitchen, not a star, not a cell, is outside him. And then, light: in him was life, and the life was the light of men. "And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." Comprehend is a lovely double word. It can mean understand, and it can mean grasp, seize, get hold of. The darkness didn't understand the light, and it couldn't get hold of it either. Translators have argued for centuries which John meant; many think both. Saint Augustine remembered the old priest Simplicianus telling him that a Platonist philosopher used to say these opening lines deserved to be written in letters of gold and set up in every church. On Christmas Day the Church reads them at Mass, so that the baby in the manger is heard with this first: before Bethlehem, the Word.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING, AGAIN.` · `LOGOS: WORD, REASON, MEANING.` · `ALL THINGS WERE MADE BY HIM.` · `THE DARKNESS DID NOT COMPREHEND IT.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle in the dark. If you can, turn off the lights and light a candle, or simply switch on one small lamp in a dark room, or picture it. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light. Notice that the dark doesn't push it out. Notice how far one small flame reaches. Let the words come back slowly: the light shineth in darkness. If you pray, you can rest in that line. If you don't, just stay with the flame and the dark around it. The bell holds the time.
Logos. Greek for word, reason, meaning. John's name for the one who was with God in the beginning, and who was God. Today's word.
Your line: the word was god. Today, when you turn on a light in a dark room, let it remind you of the first line of John. Day four hundred ninety-two.

493.title: The Word was made flesh (John 1:9–14)
493.hook: and dwelt among us; Catholics once genuflected at this line in nearly every Mass
493.howItsDone: Catholics bow at the words of the Incarnation in the Creed and genuflect there on Christmas and the Annunciation; many kneel at "and the Word was made flesh" when praying the Angelus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, logos: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. Your line was the word was god. Did a light in a dark room bring it back? Day four hundred ninety-three.

Picture a small stone church a hundred years ago. The Mass is over, or nearly. The priest has given the blessing, and now he walks to the left side of the altar and begins reading in Latin from the first chapter of John. The people are standing. Most of them don't follow every word, but they know where this is going. They are waiting for one line. When it comes, the whole room drops to one knee at once: farmers, children, old women, the priest himself. Then they stand again. Today, the line that made a church kneel.
screen: `A STONE CHURCH, A CENTURY AGO.` → `THE PRIEST READS JOHN IN LATIN.` → `EVERYONE KNEELS AT ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Before the line, John tells a hard truth. The true light came into the world, and the world, made by him, didn't know him. "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." But some did, and to them he gave power to become children of God. And then the line: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Latin, Et Verbum caro factum est. That's where they knelt. Yesterday the Word was with God before creation. Today the same Word has skin, and hunger, and a mother. Flesh is a blunt word on purpose. John could have said a body, or a human nature. He chose the word for the soft, mortal, breakable stuff we're made of. Then dwelt. The Greek verb literally means pitched his tent. It's the word for living in a tent, and Jewish readers would think of the tabernacle in the desert, the tent where God's glory came to dwell among Israel. John goes on: "and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." This is what the Church calls the Incarnation, from the Latin for in the flesh. The genuflection at the Last Gospel is mostly gone now, since that reading left the ordinary Mass in the 1960s. But the gesture lives on. In the Creed, at the words about the Son becoming man, Catholics bow. And on Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation, they kneel at those words instead. Many still pray the Angelus three times a day, and kneel at this very line. The body bends at the moment God is said to take a body.
screen: `HIS OWN RECEIVED HIM NOT.` · `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.` · `DWELT: HE PITCHED HIS TENT.` · `STILL WE BOW AT THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow at the words. Stand, if you can, or sit tall. Settle, and breathe. Say the words slowly, in your head or out loud: and the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. At made flesh, bow your head, or bend at the waist, or kneel if that's your way. Hold the bow for a breath. Then come back up and sit with what your body just did. If you pray, let the bow be your prayer. If you don't, just notice what it is to bend your body at a thought. The bell holds the time.
The Word was made flesh. John's line for the Incarnation: the eternal Word took on a human body and lived among us. Today's word.
screen: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: and dwelt among us. Today, notice one place you live, a kitchen, a desk, a car, and remember that the Word chose an address too. Day four hundred ninety-three.

fork.reveal: John chose flesh, the blunt word for soft, mortal stuff, and dwelt, literally pitched his tent among us.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Word was made flesh is a poetic way of saying Christmas.
what it means: the eternal Word, who is God, took on real human flesh and lived among people.

494.title: Come and see (John 1:29–39)
494.hook: John points, two disciples follow, and Jesus asks what seek you
494.howItsDone: At every Mass the Lamb of God (Agnus Dei) is sung or said while the priest breaks the host, and just before Communion he holds it up and repeats John the Baptist's words, behold the Lamb of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that made a church kneel: the Word was made flesh. Your line was and dwelt among us. Where did you notice the place you live? Day four hundred ninety-four.

At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest lifts the host and says a line that every Catholic in the pews knows by heart: behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. Where does that line come from? Not from a council or a liturgist. It comes from a riverbank. A man in camel hair, standing in the Jordan, sees someone walking toward him and points. Today we stand at that river and hear it said for the first time, and watch what two people do the moment they hear it.
screen: `THE HOST LIFTED AT MASS.` → `A LINE EVERY CATHOLIC KNOWS.` → `FIRST SAID AT A RIVER.`

segments.voice: John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." Lamb of God is today's word, and it's a strange thing to call a man. To a Jewish listener of the time, a lamb would call up the Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt, the lambs offered every day in the temple, and Isaiah's servant, led like a lamb to the slaughter. John packs all of that into four words. The next day he says it again, and this time two of his own disciples hear him, and they simply leave him and follow Jesus. Jesus turns around, sees them trailing behind, and asks the first words he speaks in this Gospel: "What seek you?" Not who are you, not what do you believe. What are you looking for? They answer with a question of their own: Rabbi, where do you live? And he says: "Come and see." No sermon. No test. Just an invitation to come along and look. They came, and saw where he abode, and stayed with him that day; John even remembers the hour, about four in the afternoon. One of the two, the Gospel says, was Andrew. The other is never named. Many readers since early times have thought it was the writer himself, remembering the afternoon his life turned. The Church has kept John's pointing finger at the center of the Mass. The Lamb of God is sung, three times, while the bread is broken. And then the priest lifts the host, points as John pointed, and says: behold.
screen: `JOHN POINTS: BEHOLD THE LAMB.` · `PASSOVER, TEMPLE, ISAIAH.` · `WHAT SEEK YOU?` · `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer what are you seeking. Settle, and breathe. Imagine someone turning around on a path and asking you, kindly and directly: what are you looking for? Don't give the answer you think you should give. Let the real one come up. Maybe peace. Maybe a person. Maybe just rest. Maybe you don't know, and that's an answer too. Stay with it. If you pray, you can tell God plainly what you're seeking. If you don't, just let yourself hear your own answer. The bell holds the time.
Lamb of God. John the Baptist's name for Jesus at the Jordan, recalling the Passover lamb, said again at every Mass before Communion. Today's word.
Your line: come and see. Today, when someone asks you about something you love, skip the explanation and invite them to come and see it. Day four hundred ninety-four.

495.title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
495.hook: Nathanael asks can anything good come from Nazareth
495.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew on August 24, and on that day the Mass reads this Gospel of Nathanael under the fig tree, following the old tradition that they are the same man.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lamb of God at the river, and two disciples who followed. Your line was come and see. Did you invite anyone to come and see something you love? Day four hundred ninety-five.

Everybody has a town they make fun of. The one up the highway with nothing but a gas station. The neighborhood your family warned you about. The state that's the punchline of every joke. Now imagine your friend runs up, breathless, and says: we've found him, the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, and he's from there. That's what happens today. A man named Philip has just been called. He goes straight to his friend Nathanael with the news. And Nathanael, hearing the name of the hometown, says the thing all of us have said about somewhere.
screen: `EVERYONE HAS A TOWN THEY MOCK.` → `PHILIP: WE'VE FOUND HIM.` → `HE'S FROM NAZARETH.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims, Nathanael answers: "Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" Nazareth was a small village in Galilee, not named once in the Hebrew scriptures. Nobody expected anything from it. Philip doesn't argue. He uses the words he just heard from Jesus himself: come and see. And Nathanael comes. As he walks up, Jesus says of him: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile." No guile, no trickery. It's almost a joke: the man who just insulted Jesus's town is praised for being honest. He said exactly what he thought. Nathanael is startled. How do you know me? And Jesus says: before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you. We aren't told what happened under the fig tree. The text is silent. Some rabbis in later centuries describe studying the law in the shade of a fig tree, and some Christian readers imagine Nathanael was praying or reading there. But nobody knows. What matters is that Nathanael knows, and it undoes him. In one breath the skeptic says: Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the King of Israel. And Jesus smiles at how little it took: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these. A tradition held in the Church for many centuries identifies Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew. If that's right, the man who sneered at Nazareth became one of the twelve. The good thing came from the place he'd written off.
screen: `CAN ANY GOOD COME FROM NAZARETH?` · `NO GUILE: HE SAID WHAT HE THOUGHT.` · `I SAW YOU UNDER THE FIG TREE.` · `THE SKEPTIC BECOMES AN APOSTLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a place you dismiss a chance. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place you've written off. A town, a neighborhood, a school, a kind of church, a corner of the internet, even a person's whole background. Notice the little sneer that comes up with it. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it. Now picture one good person from there, real or imagined, walking toward you the way Nathanael walked toward Jesus. If you pray, you can ask to see that place more truly. The bell holds the time.
Under the fig tree. Where Jesus said he saw Nathanael before Philip called him. The Gospel never says what happened there. Today's word.
Your line: can any good thing come. Today, catch yourself once dismissing a place or a person, and answer your own question: come and see. Day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: The first sign (John 2:1–11)
496.hook: John calls miracles signs: they point past themselves
496.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Wedding at Cana as the second of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, usually on Thursdays, and often take Mary's words to the servants as a short summary of her role.

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the fig tree: a skeptic asked whether anything good could come from Nazareth. Your line was can any good thing come. Which place or person did you give a second look? Day four hundred ninety-six.

A road sign that says Chicago, 40 miles is not Chicago. Nobody pulls over and takes a selfie with it as if they've arrived. Its whole job is to point somewhere else. Today's word is sign, and it's the word John chooses, again and again, for what most of us call miracles. He doesn't call them wonders or powers. He calls them signs. And the first one happens somewhere you wouldn't expect: not in the temple, not at a sickbed, but at a village wedding in Cana of Galilee, on the third day, when the wine runs out.
screen: `A ROAD SIGN ISN'T THE CITY.` → `JOHN'S WORD FOR MIRACLES.` → `A WEDDING IN CANA.`

segments.voice: A wedding in that world could last a week, and running out of wine was a public shame for the family. Mary notices first. She says to her son, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." Just that. His answer sounds cool to our ears: woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come. But woman was a respectful address, the same word he will use for her from the cross, and Mary seems to hear something other than no. She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." They're her last recorded words in John's Gospel. There are six stone water jars, used for the Jewish rites of washing, each holding two or three measures, something like twenty or thirty gallons apiece. Fill them with water, he says. They fill them to the brim. Draw some out, and take it to the steward. The steward tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over: everyone serves the good wine first, and the poorer wine once the guests have drunk well, "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." John closes it this way: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee; and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him." Where the Douay says miracles, John's Greek says signs, semeia. That's the key to the whole Gospel. A sign isn't the destination. It points to who he is. Here, water for washing becomes wine for a feast, and much more of it than anyone needed. Saint John Paul the Second made Cana one of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, and Catholics hear Mary's words there as advice that never expires.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY, DO YE.` · `SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `NOT A MIRACLE ONLY, A SIGN.` · then, large: `THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for a sign in your day. Settle, and breathe. Go back over today slowly, like flipping through photos on your phone. Look for one small thing that pointed past itself. A kindness that came out of nowhere. A meal that tasted better than it should. A moment that felt like more than it was. Don't force it into anything big. Just notice where it pointed. If you pray, you can thank God for it. If you don't, just let it be a sign of something good. The bell holds the time.
Sign. John's word for Jesus's miracles, semeion in Greek: a deed that points past itself to who he is. The first was at Cana. Today's word.
Your line: the good wine until now. Today, save something good for later in the day, a call, a treat, a kind word, and give it when people least expect it. Day four hundred ninety-six.

497.title: Nicodemus by night (John 3:1–8)
497.hook: born again of water and the Spirit; the Church hears baptism here
497.carry: the wind bloweth where it will
497.howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads John 3:5 as speaking of baptism, the new birth by water and the Spirit, and this passage is often read at baptisms and in the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sign at Cana: water into wine. Your line was the good wine until now. Did you save something good for late in the day? Day four hundred ninety-seven.

Some questions only come out at night. At two in the morning, lying awake, you finally ask what you couldn't ask at lunch. Today a man comes to Jesus with exactly that kind of question, and John tells us he came by night. His name is Nicodemus. He's a Pharisee, a respected teacher, a ruler among his people, a serious student of the scriptures. He has seen the signs and he's honest about it. Rabbi, he says, we know you are a teacher come from God. Nobody could do these signs unless God were with him. And Jesus answers a question he hasn't asked yet.
screen: `QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.` → `A RESPECTED TEACHER.` → `RABBI, WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen, amen I say to thee, unless a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word translated again, anothen, can also mean from above. Born again, born from above. John seems to want both. Nicodemus takes it literally, and asks the obvious, almost comic question: can a grown man go back into his mother's womb? Jesus goes further: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Water and the Spirit. This is where the Catholic Church hears baptism. The Catechism calls baptism a new birth by water and the Spirit and points to this very verse. Since the earliest centuries, Christians coming up out of the font have been called newly born. Then Jesus reaches for a picture. In Greek, the word pneuma means both wind and spirit, the same word. So the line can be read two ways. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, reads it as Spirit: "The Spirit breatheth where he will; and thou hearest his voice, but thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth." Many other English Bibles, the King James among them, read it as wind, blowing wherever it will. Today's line holds that second reading. Both are faithful to the Greek, and the point is the same. You can't see the wind. You can't steer it. You hear it in the trees and you see what it moves. Nicodemus, the careful scholar, is being told that this new birth is not something he can schedule. And he doesn't vanish from the story. John will bring him back twice, the last time carrying a hundred pounds of spices to the tomb.
screen: `BORN AGAIN, BORN FROM ABOVE.` · `WATER AND THE HOLY GHOST.` · `PNEUMA: WIND AND SPIRIT.` · `NICODEMUS WILL BE BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask your question at night. Settle, and breathe. Let a question come that you usually keep for the dark. About God, about yourself, about someone you love, about what happens after. The question you'd only ask at two in the morning. Don't answer it. Just let it be asked, out loud in your head, the way Nicodemus asked his. Notice that you're allowed to ask it. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is. If you don't, just hold it honestly. The bell holds the time.
Nicodemus by night. The Pharisee and teacher who came to Jesus in the dark and heard about being born of water and the Spirit. Today's word.

Your line: the wind bloweth where it will. Today, feel the wind, or a fan, and remember what you can't control. And that's week seventy-one: great joy, logos, the Word made flesh, the Lamb of God, the fig tree, the first sign, and Nicodemus. Day four hundred ninety-seven.
